1. Pulling the head out makes it go flat, pushing it in, makes it go sharp. Find the middle ground for you

  2. Yes.

  3. Regulate your airflow and produce a steady stream of air but realize your lungs have a fixed capacity.

  4. Cover the holes fully, use a stream of steady, even airflow and don't blast. Recorders have a max volume before the body resonates too much and squeaks.
I've seen many people forgetting a question mark at the end of a question. You just did the opposite, you should have used a period.

1. I have never played an alto recorder, so I think Google or YouTube would be a better source of information for this than I would ever be.

  2. Yes. You'll build up lung capacity as you use them more. There's even discrepancies between different instruments... Flute or piccolo players end up having the best lung capacity due to the fact that such a large percentage of their expelled air ends up not even going into their instrument. When I was in band, we did a balloon test where each student got an empty balloon, was allowed to take one deep breath, and had to fill the balloon as much as they could with that one breath... the flute/piccolo players all won.

  3. There's a technique called cyclic breathing you could try. I do it with my trumpet, which helps... Also, Kenny G did it for his world record note. It's a process of filling your mouth/cheeks with air, using your mouth/cheek muscles to simulate expelling air, and taking a breath in through your nose. It's tough to keep your intonation, not break the note, and maintain pitch while just trying to breathe... also you lung capacity will expand as I stated in #2.

  4. It's hard to answer this without seeing how you play. This could be due to your breathing, embouchure, the way your instrument is put together, or the way your finger-placement is situated. I'd focus on practicing good technique, for all of these points... it's harder to learn it correctly the first time than it is to just play... but it'll be even harder than that to break yourself of bad "habits" you pick up from not doing it correctly from the beginning.
